editorial:
Abel Gance's J'accuse! is a nearly three-hour anti-war epic produced by PathÃ© FrÃ¨res in France and first screened in 1919, built around a climactic sequence in which dead soldiers rise from the battlefield and march home â€” a scene Gance filmed using actual soldiers on leave from the front. D. W. Griffith saw a New York screening in 1921 and arranged US distribution through United Artists, making this one of the earliest French films to receive wide American release. The unrestored 1919 print is free to use in the United States: the 95-year maximum US copyright term expired in 2014, and even if the URAA had restored a US copyright in 1996 (on grounds that the French production never complied with US formalities), that restoration could not survive past the 2014 ceiling. A renewal search for 1946â€“1947 is moot under this term-expiry analysis but is provided for completeness.

The practical rights trap is the 2007 Lobster Films and Nederlands Filmmuseum restoration, released in the US by Flicker Alley. That edition assembled six archival prints â€” including one reel of Gance's original camera negative â€” and added color tinting, digital stabilization, and a newly synchronized score. Every layer of that work is independently protected as a derivative work, regardless of the 1919 print's PD status. Copies circulating on the Internet Archive with 'restored' in their title or bearing Flicker Alley branding are not the public-domain print. Stick to the unrestored uploads (see watch list above) and verify no Lobster Films or Flicker Alley credit appears before incorporating any footage.
faq: The Flicker Alley restoration looks far superior to the archive prints â€” is it public domain too?

No. The 2007 Lobster Films/Nederlands Filmmuseum restoration, released in the US by Flicker Alley, is a separately copyrighted derivative work whose color-tinted images, stabilized frames, and synchronized score are not in the public domain. Only the unrestored 1919 print â€” available on Internet Archive without 'restored' in the identifier â€” is free to use in the US.
J'accuse was made in France â€” does the URAA complicate its US public-domain status?

Not anymore. The URAA (17 U.S.C. Â§ 104A) could have restored US copyright in 1996 for this French work if it lacked US registration formalities, but that restoration only ran through the remainder of the maximum US term. For a 1919 work the 95-year maximum expires in 2014, which has already passed. Any URAA-restored copyright in this title expired in 2014, and the print is unambiguously in the US public domain as of 2026.
